title: Where It Was Written
logline: A jumble of granite boulders above a main road, with caves under the overhangs, where a later tradition says a teaching carried whole in memory was first written down on leaves, although the two chronicles that record the writing-down name no place at all; the film spends a working day there on the list that teaching asks to be learned by heart, a map of every kind of moment of mind in four unequal regions, three named after worlds and the fourth after nowhere.
human_question: If a thing can be recorded exactly and still have no place attached to it, is that because somebody left the place out, or because there was never a place to give?

place.what_kind_of_place: A living rock temple built into a landslip of huge granite boulders on the edge of a valley floor, a few minutes' walk above a busy main road. The caves are the gaps and overhangs between the boulders, each with a groove cut along its brow so rain drips clear of the mouth. Tiled roofs and whitewashed fronts are tucked under the rock; inside, the caves are painted from floor to ceiling with modern murals: gods and Brahmas on arches, a mountain with four rivers running from four animal mouths, and one cave of plaster figures of monks bent over leaves. There is a small room of palm-leaf books and a small museum. Some overhangs are left bare.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Scale and contrast in one sightline: boulders the size of houses standing over a road full of buses, stalls and school groups, with painted caves pressed into the gaps between them. Inside a few metres the picture goes from traffic and noise, to walls crowded with painted figures, to an overhang of plain grey rock with nothing on it but the drip line and lichen. Add a room of books made of palm leaf, bound between boards, and the scratch of a stylus if a leaf-writer can be filmed, and the site gives three very different textures of picture without leaving the rock.
place.what_moves_or_changes: Only the ordinary day. Traffic and people on the road; visitors arriving and leaving by the steps; sun and shade moving across the boulders; the temple's own routine, heard more than seen. Nothing is staged and nothing has a schedule the crew can control except the temple's opening and closing.
place.when_it_looks_best: A dry-season weekday, from mid-morning to closing time. The film needs no particular light: it avoids sunrise, sunset and any light event, and works in sun or in cloud. It needs the road busy and the caves open.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A day on a rock above a road. The film cuts between a small number of fixed camera positions and keeps coming back to them in a set rotation: the road at the foot of the rock, loud and crowded; a painted arch inside a cave, full of figures; a bare overhang with nothing painted on it; and, in between, a room of leaf-books bound between boards and a cave of plaster monks writing. It ends at the end of the working day with the road emptying. Without a word of narration it is a clear piece about a crowded world, a painted world and a blank one, stacked a few metres apart, and it has a shape: morning to closing time, noise to quiet and back.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The voice gives the rotation its meaning without adding anything the screen does not show. The list these films keep returning to, the one the handbook says must be learned by heart, is a map in four unequal regions; the books name the first three after worlds where such moments are mostly at home, and say of the fourth that there is no place of that name at all. The rock carries the same question as history: a teaching carried in memory was written down, the two chronicles that record it give no place, and the place was supplied some thirteen hundred years later by Sinhala texts with their own reasons for supplying it. The film separates the two kinds of missing place, one left out and one that the books say was never there, and fills the fourth region's share of its running time with pictures from the other three, saying plainly that they are not pictures of it.

sequence.on_screen: Station one, mid-morning. 35 mm at standing eye height, locked on the main road at the foot of the rock: a bus braking, a three-wheeler, a fruit stall, a school group crossing seen from behind, and above all of it the grey boulders with whitewash and tiled roofs tucked underneath. The camera pans only to follow something that moves and stops when it has gone.
sequence.voice: There is a list these films keep coming back to. It sorts every kind of moment of mind that the old books recognise, and one of the modern Sinhala handbooks that set it out tells the student, without softening it, to get the whole of it by heart so that it cannot be forgotten, because if it is forgotten the rest of the study cannot be done. For a long time that was how the whole teaching was kept: not written on anything, but carried by people who had learned it.

sequence.on_screen: The leaf-book room, daylight from the doorway only, 50 mm locked: stacks of palm-leaf volumes between wooden boards, tied with cord, on plain shelves. Nothing is opened, handled or brought out. If a trained leaf-writer has agreed to be filmed, a second shot: two hands only, a stylus cutting lines into a pale leaf that show almost nothing, then a cloth of soot and oil wiped across it and the letters coming up black.
sequence.voice: Two chronicles record the moment it stopped being only that. In the reign of Vattagamani, they say, the monks who had until then carried the three baskets of the teaching and the commentaries by mouth came together and wrote them down in books, so that the teaching would last. One gives the reason as the people falling away; the other as the decline of beings. That is the whole account, two verses in each. It names no place. It gives no number of monks and no leader.

sequence.on_screen: The cave of plaster figures, locked, eye height: a row of modern monks in plaster and paint, bent over leaves with styluses, lit by the doorway. Then back to station one for three shots of the road, then the steps from below with visitors coming up them, seen from behind.
sequence.voice: This cave shows the scene anyway. The place enters writing about thirteen hundred years after the event, in a Sinhala book of the thirteenth century, the Pujavaliya, which says in one line that in that king's day five hundred arahants lived at a cave of this temple's name and held a recital of the books. A little over a century later the Nikaya Sangrahaya adds the district, the patronage of an unnamed local chief, and that they recited the texts and wrote them down; it also puts the writing before a rival monastery broke away, and lists the unbroken line of elders who had carried it, so the first books belong to the line that stayed. Where a book was first written down is a claim about whose book it is. A second cave of the same name, in another district, keeps the same tradition. This film does not decide between them.

sequence.on_screen: Station two, inside a painted cave, locked, 35 mm: an arch crowded with figures, a Brahma riding a goose at its centre, gods on either side. Then the painted mountain on the same rock with four rivers running out of the mouths of a lion, an elephant, a horse and a peacock. Ordinary shot lengths; no move.
sequence.voice: The list itself is a map. The books divide every moment of mind into four regions, and name the first three after the worlds where such moments mostly arise: the world of the senses, which in their scheme holds that road and everyone on it; the world of fine form, where figures like the one on this arch are said to live; and the formless world. The word they use is mostly. A moment belongs to its region by where it is at home, not by where it turns up. And they are frank that the mind is one thing in its nature, and is divided like this only so that it can be taught.

sequence.on_screen: Station three, an overhang nobody has painted, locked, 35 mm, looking up at the underside of the rock: the drip groove cut along the brow, grey granite, lichen, a stain where the water runs. Then station two again, then station three again, cut at the same rhythm as the road.
sequence.voice: The painters here gave figures to the first two regions. They had nothing to give the third: the books say the beings of the formless world have no body at all, only mind, so there is nothing to paint. The regions are not equal. By the handbook's count the first holds fifty-four kinds of moment, the second fifteen, the third twelve. The fourth is counted as eight, or, looked at more closely, as forty: the same heap counted finer. And the books say something about the fourth that they say about none of the others. There is no place called that. The name is given to the moments themselves.

sequence.on_screen: The outside of the rock in full afternoon: whitewash laid straight onto granite, a tiled roof hard against an overhang, the dark streaks under the drip lines. Cut in full frame, the same boulders photographed in 1896, then the present angle again. Then the doorway of the cave kept for Buddhaghosa, from outside, not entered.
sequence.voice: Everything on this rock has been altered by what works against it, which is how the books define matter: heat and cold, rain, fire. In 1848, in fighting in the country round about, British troops came to this temple and its library burned; the temple's own account and every later one say so. The painting now in these caves is later than that, and a photograph of 1896 already shows some of it. The leaves on the shelves inside were cut between 1981 and 1991. This cave is given to Buddhaghosa, the commentator; the chronicle that tells his story puts him at work in the capital and says nothing of this rock. The film leaves each of these in the order it came.

sequence.on_screen: The last minute adds no new position. It takes its pictures from the same three stations in the same rotation as the rest of the film: the road, the painted arch, the bare overhang, the road. The working day ends in them: a stall packing up, a bus pulling out, the steps with nobody on them. The last frame is the road, at ordinary length, and it cuts.
sequence.voice: That is a different kind of missing from the chronicle's. The chronicle left the place out; the books say there is none to leave out. The moments they put in the fourth region happen, they say, inside the other three and belong to none of them, and what those moments turn to is the one thing in their scheme that nothing made. So the fourth region's share of this film has been filled from the other three, and these pictures are not of it. They are the road, the arch and the rock again. Whatever was written here, burned here and shelved here since, the handbook still asks for the list in the same way: by heart. It comes to a place like this in people, and at the end of the day it leaves in them.

concept_merge.why_together: C018 is the whole map at once and an instruction about how to hold it: the Margaya lists every type sphere by sphere, 54 sense-sphere, 15 fine-material, 12 immaterial and 40 supramundane, and tells the student to make the list fluent so that it cannot be forgotten, because further study depends on it [C018-M:L3; C018-M:L125]. The Pradeepika counts the same set as 89 or 121 depending on how finely the supramundane is counted [C018-P:L23–L25]. That instruction is the film's history: a teaching held by heart, and the moment it was put onto leaves. C003 supplies the map's geography and its one strange region: mind is one in its nature and divided only to be taught [C003-M:L5]; it is divided into four by plane [C003-M:L9]; the first three are named for the worlds where such minds mostly arise [C003-M:L11–L19]; and of the fourth the Margaya says there is no place called the supramundane plane, the name being given to the supramundane states themselves [C003-M:L17], whose minds arise in all three planes without belonging to them [C003-M:L19]. The Pradeepika adds that the formless worlds have no bodily form, only mind [C003-P:L97], which is why the third region can be named and not painted. C002 closes the film honestly: three of the four ultimates are conditioned and break up, and the fourth is unconditioned and realised through the path with great effort [C002-M:L21; C002-P:L46], while matter is what is struck and altered by opposing conditions such as heat and cold [C002-P:L40; C002-M:L17], which is the only thing the rock, the paint and the leaves have ever been.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: Two kinds of missing place that a careless film would merge. The chronicles leave out where the teaching was written down; that is a gap in a record, and later writers filled it, for reasons of their own. The books leave the fourth region without a place because, they say, it has none; that is not a gap to be filled, and no later painter on this rock filled it. C018 alone would make a film about memorising a list; C003 alone a film about a cosmology; C002 alone a film about impermanent matter. Together they make the list something that was carried, written, burned and rewritten, while its fourth region stayed exactly where the books put it, which is nowhere. The pairing also blocks the cheap ending, because C003's fourth region is minds, which C002 counts among the made things, turned towards the one thing C002 says is not made, and neither can be photographed; the film says so instead of offering a beautiful frame in its place.

concept_links.why: This is the only story found that turns on C018's own question: one whole map, carried by heart, divided into four unequal regions. The Margaya's instruction to get the 121 by heart so it is never forgotten, because further study depends on it [C018-M:L3], is the condition the teaching was kept in until it was written down, and the rock is where a later tradition puts that change. The four regions and their unequal sizes are narrated once, as a list and never as a sum [C018-M:L125], and the two counts, eight or forty for the fourth, are called the same heap counted finer, as the Pradeepika's totals allow [C018-P:L23–L25]. The digest's limits are kept: no one is asked which type they are; the regions are regions of moments, not a ladder of people; 'unwholesome' is never a verdict on anyone; the supramundane is never a peak experience; and the film does not dwell on the arithmetic, which the digest warns turns a film into a lecture. The film must also not claim that this list was among what was written down here: the chronicles speak of the three pitakas and the commentaries, and the compendium and handbooks that set out the 121 are many centuries later.

C003 gives the map its geography and its one region with no ground. The Margaya divides mind into four by plane [C003-M:L9], names the first three for where such minds mostly arise, with the word 'mostly' doing real work [C003-M:L11–L19], and says flatly that there is no place called the supramundane plane; the supramundane states themselves are given that name [C003-M:L17]. Their minds arise in all three planes without belonging to them [C003-M:L19], which is the film's licence for filling the fourth region's share of its running time with pictures from the other three. The Pradeepika's formless worlds, with no bodily form and only mind [C003-P:L97], explain why the painted rock has figures for two regions and nothing for the third. Its definition of supramundane minds as path and fruit minds that take nibbāna as object [C003-P:L143] keeps the voice exact about what the fourth region holds. The digest's limits are carried: the lower planes are spoken of as the books' abodes of beings, never as 'higher states of consciousness'; the fourth is never a mood; and the teaching that mind is one and divided only to be taught [C003-M:L5] is narrated as the books' own frankness about their method, not as a modern slogan.

C002 sets the film's limit and its material. The rock, the whitewash, the paint and the leaves are all matter in the sources' sense, what is struck and altered by opposing conditions such as heat and cold [C002-P:L40; C002-M:L17], which is the whole of what happened here in 1848 and since, told as layers rather than as loss. The fourth ultimate is unconditioned, and the sources say it is realised by noble ones through the path and great effort [C002-M:L21; C002-P:L46]; so the film cannot show it and says so, and never lets a quiet cave, a bare overhang or the end of the day stand in for it. The digest's limits are kept: nibbāna is not calm, relaxation or extinction; nothing is called unreal; and the fourth region of C003, which is minds, is not confused with the unconditioned they turn to.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That the map of mind at the centre of this series is a thing people carried whole in their heads before it was ever written, that the books themselves divide it into four unequal regions and name three of them after worlds, and that the fourth has no place because the books say it has none, which is a different thing from a chronicle forgetting to say where something happened. The viewer also sees, without being told how to feel about it, that a place can be attached to an event centuries later and that the attaching is itself a claim.
what_must_be_real: The road, the visitors and the temple's day as they are; nobody arranged, nobody asked to repeat anything. No monk or visitor is filmed close, identified, interviewed or framed in any state of mind, and no act of worship is interrupted, restarted or lit. Nothing in the leaf-book room is opened, handled, brought out or displayed for the camera; if a trained leaf-writer is filmed, it is at work they already do, hands only, with their consent, and if no such work exists the shot is cut, not staged. The plaster council figures are filmed as what they are, a modern depiction of a tradition. The hell-punishment murals are not filmed. The 1896 photograph is used as an archival insert and captioned only by the voice. The tradition that the writing-down happened here is never narrated as fact; the voice attributes it to the texts that carry it, with their dates. No date or text is used to rank this temple against the other cave of the same name.
position_hint: Late in GRP-01, as the first sight of the whole map before the series walks through it region by region; it is the last film in the group to talk about names and the first to show the four regions the later groups open. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: Shared site: IDEA-0079 (GRP-05, pending) currently also stands on this rock and also narrates the writing-down, the 1848 fire and the 1981 to 1991 rewriting. The two films must not both be made as they stand. That film is to be moved when GRP-05 is reworked; until then, the overlap is recorded here and in connections, and 0079 is not edited from this record.

Treating the tradition as history. The chronicles name no place, number, leader or duration; the place and the five hundred arrive in the thirteenth century and the district a little over a century later. Every sentence about the site's role must carry its source.
A second cave of the same name in another district keeps the same tradition. The film records that it exists and does not rank the two; it must not become a contest between temples.
The 1848 layer turning into a grievance or remembrance register, or the rebellion becoming the subject. It is one layer among several, in one sentence, with no adjectives.

Overclaiming the link between the list and the event. The 121 is set out in a compendium and in handbooks written many centuries after the writing-down; the film says the teaching was carried by heart and that the handbook still asks for the list by heart, and never that this list was written down here.
Arithmetic. The counts are said once, as a list; no sum is spoken, no table is shown and the editing proportions that follow the map's shares are never pointed out.

Implying the fourth region, or the unconditioned, through a picture: a bare overhang, an empty cave, a closing door, the quiet at closing time. The last beat says in words that the pictures are not of it, and the last frame is the road, not a view.
Confusing C003's fourth region (supramundane minds, which are conditioned) with C002's fourth ultimate (the unconditioned). The voice keeps them apart.
Kamma as fate: the hell murals depict punishments as deserved outcomes and are kept out of the film entirely.

Monks as exhibit. The temple is a living monastery. Monks are not filmed close or named, the routine is heard more than seen, and the 1981 to 1991 work is narrated as a fact about the books, not as a portrait.

Treatment collisions inside GRP-01 and on the slate. No drone, no dawn, no sunrise or sunset payoff, no raking light on the painted walls, no long holds, no continuous move, no tilt into empty air, no macro payoff, no zoom, no time-lapse and no heat haze; the rotation between fixed stations at ordinary shot lengths is the film's own grammar.
The district is closed at 7 on the true count; this film takes it to 8 until IDEA-0079 moves. It is also the second GRP-01 film in the district, after IDEA-0003.
Buddhaghosa's association with the site is tradition only. The voice says so and says what the chronicle does record.
drop_if: The temple does not agree to filming in the painted caves and the leaf-book room on an ordinary day, or will allow it only with arranged activity.
The station-one road view cannot be taken without filming identifiable people close; the road must read as traffic, not as portraits.

IDEA-0079 is kept at this site when GRP-05 is reworked. Then one of the two films has to move, and since this is C018's only carrier found, the case for keeping this one should be put to Chathura rather than decided by default.
The leaf-writing shot is available only as a performance for visitors; it is then cut, and beat 2 runs on the closed volumes alone.

connections.note: Same rock, same event. That film (GRP-05, pending) follows one bell stroke at first light out across the valley, flies or long-lenses over the roofs, and carries the writing-down, the fire and the rewriting as its second scale for a concept about what starts a mind-door process. This one never leaves the rock, has no bell, no dawn and no valley flight, and uses the writing-down for C018's whole map held in memory and the dispute over where it happened. They cannot both be made at this site; that film is due to be moved when GRP-05 is reworked, and nothing in it has been changed from this record.

Both films reach the fourth ultimate at the end. That one names it and says it is the one thing it can name and not show, over the open sea. This one does not use that line: it fills the fourth region's share of its running time with ordinary pictures from the other three and says they are not of it, and it ends on a road, not a view.

Forty thousand years of people under one overhang, none of them named and nothing written; here, a teaching kept entirely by people until it was written, and a place name attached to the writing thirteen centuries later. One film has lives and no names; this one has a name and a disputed place for it.

The other GRP-01 film in the same district, on a rock citadel with painted figures and centuries of visitors' verses scratched into a wall. That one reads painted figures that nobody can name; this one uses painted figures only as figures for two regions of a map, and films no writing on any wall.

selection.reason: GRP-01's only carrier for C018. A fresh search across the open districts found no other place whose documented story turns on one whole map, learned by heart, divided into four unequal regions, one of which is not a place; this rock does, and its dispute over where the writing-down happened is the other half of the same question. It is kept on those grounds despite the closed district and the shared site, both recorded in risks and research_note. This field records executed merges only.

review.note: Chathura reopened this slot on 2026-09-26 after the GRP-01 audit. The earlier body, set at a reservoir, was set aside, and a blind search of the open districts found no location that carries C018, the primary concept. On 2026-09-27 Aluvihare was chosen as the only candidate found that carries C018, the decision being delegated by Chathura, with the district allowed to 8 temporarily because IDEA-0079 at the same site is to be moved when GRP-05 is reworked. The body was then rewritten from new research: title, location, treatment, beats, historical thread and connections are all new; the concepts and their order are unchanged. The previous status was pending and it stays pending under standing decision 9, because the body has been replaced and has not been reviewed. What most needs his eye: whether he accepts the shared site and the eighth Matale film until 0079 moves; whether the rotation-between-stations treatment reads as distinct from every other GRP-01 film; and the ground checks listed in unknowns, above all filming permission in the painted caves and the leaf-book room.

suggested_location.region: Matale District, Central Province: on the west side of the Matale valley, beside the Matale to Dambulla road (A9), about three kilometres north of Matale town and about thirty kilometres north of Kandy. Reverse geocoding of the coordinates returns Aluwihare, Matale, Matale District.
suggested_location.why_here: Because the story at this rock already asks C018's question and the rock gives the camera three kinds of picture a few metres apart. The teaching the list belongs to was carried whole in memory until it was written down, and the two chronicles that record the writing-down give no place for it; the place was supplied by Sinhala texts of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, which placed it here, and a second cave of the same name elsewhere keeps the same tradition. That gives the film a place that is itself a claim, which is exactly the contrast it needs with the map's fourth region, which the books say has no place at all. Physically the rock is a landslip of granite boulders standing over a main road, with painted caves in the gaps between them and bare overhangs beside the painted ones: a crowded world, a painted world with gods and Brahmas on it, and plain rock with nothing to paint, which lets the film give the map's first three regions three different stations without a single diagram, and give the fourth none.

historical_thread.story:
Two chronicles record the writing-down, and neither says where it happened. The Dipavamsa, the older of the two, compiled around the fourth century CE, says at XX.20-21, in Oldenberg's 1879 translation, that before this time the wise bhikkhus had orally handed down the text of the three pitakas and the atthakatha, and that at this time the bhikkhus who perceived the decay of created beings assembled and, in order that the religion might endure for a long time, recorded them in written books. The Pali behind 'decay of created beings' is haniṃ disvana sattanaṃ. The Mahavamsa, compiled in the fifth or sixth century, says the same at XXXIII.100-101, in Geiger's 1912 translation: 'The text of the three pitakas and the atthakatha thereon did the most wise bhikkhus hand down in former times orally, but since they saw that the people were falling away (from religion) the bhikkhus came together, and in order that the true doctrine might endure, they wrote them down in books.' Both passages close the reign of Vattagamani Abhaya, who lost his capital to invaders, spent some fourteen years out of it, and took it back. Neither names a place, a number of monks, a leader, a patron or a duration, and neither gives a famine or failing memory as the reason; the reason given is the falling away of people or the decline of beings. In the Mahavamsa the two verses come immediately after the account of the Abhayagiri monks seceding from the Theravada, and Geiger's own note on the chapter reads the author's word 'here' as 'out of the Mahavihara'. Geiger adds no note on where the writing took place.

The place enters writing in Sinhala. The Pujavaliya, the devotional compendium of Mayurapada Buddhaputra Thera, conventionally dated to 1266 in the Dambadeniya period, gives in its chapter of royal histories one sentence under Vattagamani, after recording that the famine called Bamini-tiya sāya happened in his time: 'mōvun davasa pansiyayak rahatan vahansē alulena vædahiňda pot saňgāyanā kaḷa sēka', in his day five hundred arahants, residing at Alulena, held a recital of the books. It names the cave. It does not name a district, and its verb is saňgāyanā, a recital or council, not the verb for writing. A little over a century later the Nikaya Sangrahaya, the history of the Order written by the elder Jayabahu, formerly Devarakshita, which runs to the fifteenth year of Bhuvanekabahu V and is usually dated to the 1390s, gives the full scene. In the 1908 English translation: 'At that time 500 Arahats who assembled at Alulvihāra in the country of Mātale, under the patronage of a certain chief, recited, and reduced to writing the text of the Three Piṭakas', 'leaving nothing, adding nothing, free from all heresy', 'the same which had been brought down orally in the succession of the great monks' Upali, Dasaka, Sonaka, Siggava, Moggaliputta-Tissa, Mahinda and thirty-odd others, to Sivasthavira. Only after that does it tell the founding of Abhayagiri and the secession of Mahadaeliya-Tissa's following, which it dates to the fifteenth year of the reign. So between the thirteenth and the late fourteenth centuries the tradition acquires a cave, a number, a district, a patron and the act of writing, and in the fullest version the writing is placed before the schism and credited to the lineage that stayed.

Who gained by that is a question, not a finding, and the film asks it only as a question. Both texts were written by monks of the Mahavihara tradition, the Nikaya Sangrahaya expressly as a history of that lineage and of the Order's purifications. Setting the first written canon outside the capital, before the split, in the hands of an unbroken line of Theravada elders, makes the written books the property of that line and of no rival monastery; setting it in the hill country also gives the hill-country monasteries of the writers' own day a founding claim that the capital had lost. H. W. Cave, writing in 1897, already read the event this way, saying the convention 'had in view also the provision of means of combating the heresy of the Abhayagiriya fraternity'; that is his reading, not a source's. Later retellings add more: a leader named as Maharakkhita in some accounts and Kunthagattha Tissa of the Thuparama in others, a duration of three years or of three years, three months and three weeks, a finish on a Vesak full moon, copies deposited here and at Abhayagiri, the name 'Fourth Council', and an etymology from aloka, light. None of these is in the chronicles and none was found in the two earliest texts that name the place.

The name itself has a collision. A second temple called Alulena, in Kegalle District, keeps a local tradition that the Tripitaka was written there in Vattagamani's reign, and the Pujavaliya's 'Alulena' names no district. It is the Nikaya Sangrahaya's 'country of Mātale' that fixes the tradition on this rock.

The association with Buddhaghosa is the same kind of layer. One cave here is dedicated to him and popular and guidebook accounts say he visited, checked commentaries or spent years here. The Culavamsa's account of him (chapter 37 in Geiger's numbering) brings him from India to the Mahavihara in the capital, to its great practising-house, where he learned the Sinhala commentary from Sanghapala, wrote the Visuddhimagga and read it out near the Great Bodhi Tree; it says nothing of this rock. The earliest source found for his presence here is a 2006 newspaper feature, which says only 'it is on record'.

The nineteenth century is a layer of damage, recorded as such. The rebellion of July 1848 in the country round Matale was put down under martial law, and every modern account of the site, the temple's own, the provincial tourism department's, the standard guides and the 2006 and 2019 Sunday Times features, says that British troops came to the temple in the course of it and that the library burned with the loss of many manuscripts. No account from 1848 or the years just after it was located for this record, and Cave's 1897 description of the site does not mention the damage, so the event is reported here as attested by later accounts, and the amount destroyed is not given. Cave's photographs of 1896 show the rock temple and painted surfaces; the murals now in the caves are described by a recent photographer as all modern.

The present is a layer of rewriting. Between 1981 and 1991, under the chief incumbent Ven. Ethipola Medhankara Nayaka Thera, the Tipitaka was written out again on talipot leaf at the temple by an ayurvedic physician and four others who knew leaf writing; those volumes are kept in the temple's library and shown in its small museum. On 5 January 2019 the Tripitaka was declared a national heritage at a ceremony at the temple, with a stated intention of seeking UNESCO recognition. Whether leaf writing is still done at the temple, and by whom, was not established.
historical_thread.how_it_binds:
C018 is an instruction as much as a list. The Margaya ends the first chapter by laying out every type of consciousness, sphere by sphere, 54 and 15 and 12 and 40, and telling the student to get it fluent so that it is never forgotten, because if it is forgotten the rest cannot be learned [C018-M:L3; C018-M:L125]. That instruction describes the condition the whole teaching was in for its first centuries on the island, according to both chronicles: carried by mouth and held by heart. This rock is where a later tradition says that condition ended. The film does not claim the 121 was among what was written; the list is set out in a compendium and handbooks many centuries later, and the chronicles speak of the three pitakas and their commentaries. It claims only what the sources support: that the map it names is still asked for by heart, and that the teaching it belongs to was once kept no other way.

The second binding is C003's, and it is the reason this story rather than any other memorised text. The map has four regions and the books name three of them after places: the sense world, the fine-material world, the formless world, where such minds mostly arise [C003-M:L11–L19]. Of the fourth the Margaya says there is no place of that name; the supramundane states themselves are called its plane [C003-M:L17], and their minds arise in all three worlds without belonging to any [C003-M:L19]. The rock's own history is a record without a place: the chronicles that record the writing-down give none, and one was supplied later. Put side by side, the two show the difference the film is about. A place missing from a chronicle is a gap; later writers could fill it, and did, with their own reasons. A place missing from the map is not a gap; the books say there was never one to fill. The painted caves make the same point in pigment. Painters gave figures to the sense world and to the fine-material Brahmas; the formless worlds, the Pradeepika says, have no bodily form at all [C003-P:L97], so there is nothing to paint; and the fourth region is not a world to paint in the first place.

C002 governs what the camera may claim. Rock, whitewash, paint and leaf are matter, which the sources define by its being struck and altered by opposing conditions such as heat and cold [C002-P:L40; C002-M:L17], and the site's history of fire, repainting and rewriting is that definition at work, told as layers. The fourth ultimate is unconditioned and realised only through the path by great effort [C002-M:L21; C002-P:L46]; the fourth region of C003 is the minds that take it as object [C003-P:L143]. Neither can be filmed, so the film does not try: it gives the fourth region its share of running time and fills it, as C003-M:L19 permits, with pictures from the other three, and says aloud that they are not of it.
what_is_certain: The Dipavamsa, XX.20-21 in Oldenberg's 1879 edition and translation, records that before Vattagamani's time the bhikkhus had orally handed down the text of the three pitakas and the atthakatha, and that at this time the bhikkhus 'who perceived the decay of created beings' assembled and recorded them in written books so that the religion might endure. It names no place.

The Mahavamsa, XXXIII.100-101 in Geiger's 1912 translation, records the same in two verses, giving the reason as 'the people were falling away (from religion)'. It names no place, number, leader, patron or duration, and gives no famine or failing memory as the reason. The verses directly follow the account of the Abhayagiri secession. Geiger's 1912 edition carries no note on where the writing took place.

The Pujavaliya (Mayurapada Buddhaputra Thera, conventionally 1266), in its chapter of royal histories, says under Vattagamani that the famine called Bamini-tiya sāya happened in his time and that in his day five hundred arahants, residing at Alulena, held a saňgāyanā of the books. It names the cave, not the district, and uses the word for recital or council, not for writing. Checked in the Sinhala text at pitaka.lk.

The Nikaya Sangrahaya of Jayabahu (formerly Devarakshita), which runs to the fifteenth year of Bhuvanekabahu V and is dated to the 1390s, says in the 1908 English translation that 500 Arahats 'who assembled at Alulvihāra in the country of Mātale, under the patronage of a certain chief, recited, and reduced to writing the text of the Three Piṭakas', lists the elders who had carried it orally, and places the founding of Abhayagiri and the secession afterwards. Checked in the translation at ancient-buddhist-texts.net.

The Culavamsa's account of Buddhaghosa (ch. 37, Geiger's translation) places him at the Mahavihara in the capital, learning the Sinhala commentary from Sanghapala and writing the Visuddhimagga; it does not mention this site.

H. W. Cave's The Ruined Cities of Ceylon (1897; edition of 1904 checked) describes the cave as the scene of Vattagamani's convention of monks and says the convention also aimed at 'combating the heresy of the Abhayagiriya fraternity'. It does not mention damage in 1848. Cave's photographs of the site are dated 1896 in the Rijksmuseum's records.

The 1848 rebellion in the Matale country broke out at the end of July 1848 and martial law was declared; modern accounts of the site, including the temple's own as reported, the Sunday Times features of 2006 and 2019 and Wikipedia's article citing History.lk, state that British troops attacked the temple and the library burned.

Between 1981 and 1991 the Tipitaka was written out again on talipot leaf at the temple under the chief incumbent Ven. Ethipola Medhankara Nayaka Thera by an ayurvedic physician and four others, and the volumes are kept in the library (Sunday Times, 3 September 2006).
On 5 January 2019 the Tripitaka was declared a national heritage at a ceremony at the temple, with a stated intention of seeking UNESCO recognition (Sunday Times, 6 January 2019).

The site is in Matale District: the coordinates reverse-geocode to Aluwihare, Matale, Matale District, Central Province, beside the Matale to Dambulla road, about three kilometres north of Matale town.
what_is_disputed: That the writing-down happened at this rock at all. It rests on the Pujavaliya (cave named, no district, a recital) and the Nikaya Sangrahaya (district named, recital and writing), written some thirteen and fourteen centuries after the event; the chronicles are silent on the place. Their silence is not a denial, and the film does not treat it as one; it treats the placing as a later claim.

Which Alulena. A temple of that name in Kegalle District keeps a local tradition that the writing happened there. The Pujavaliya names no district; the Nikaya Sangrahaya's 'country of Mātale' points here. Not adjudicated, and the film does not rank the two temples.

The details added in modern retellings and often attributed to the Mahavamsa, which does not contain them: a leader named Maharakkhita or Kunthagattha Tissa, a patron who was a local ruler or the king, a duration of three years or three years, three months and three weeks, completion on a Vesak full moon, copies at this site and at Abhayagiri, the numbering as the Fourth (or Fifth) Council, and a record of thirty or thirty-eight generations in an 'Asgiri' leaf document. None was found in the sources checked; the Asgiri document was not seen.
The etymology from aloka, light. The two earliest texts checked write Alulena and Alulvihāra; the aloka derivation appears only in modern accounts.

The famine as the cause. The Pujavaliya puts the famine in the same reign; modern accounts, and IDEA-0079's current voice, make it and the invasion the reason for the writing. Neither chronicle gives that reason.
Buddhaghosa at this site. Tradition, a cave dedicated to him, and guidebook and newspaper statements ('it is on record') only; the chronicle that tells his story places him in the capital.

The extent of the 1848 damage. All accounts found are modern; no account from 1848 or its aftermath was located, and Cave in 1897 does not mention it. How much burned is described differently in different places and is not stated here.

Who gained. The reading that placing the written canon here, before the schism, strengthened the Mahavihara lineage's claim to it, and gave hill-country monasteries a founding claim, is an inference from what the texts do and from who wrote them, shared by Cave in 1897. No source states the motive.

what_to_film: Station one: the main road at the foot of the rock from a fixed position at standing height, with the boulders, roofs and whitewash above it; traffic and people as traffic, never as portraits.
Station two: one painted arch with a Brahma on a goose and gods on either side, and the painted mountain with four rivers from four animal mouths; locked, ordinary shot lengths, no raking light.
Station three: an unpainted overhang looking up at the underside of the rock and the drip groove along its brow.

The leaf-book room from the doorway, closed volumes between boards, nothing opened; and, only if it is work a trained leaf-writer already does and consents to, their hands cutting a leaf and wiping soot across it.
The cave of plaster monks writing on leaves, as a modern depiction.
The outside of the rock in afternoon light, and the same boulders in Cave's 1896 photograph as an archival insert.
The doorway of the cave dedicated to Buddhaghosa, from outside only.
The end of the working day at the three stations, for the last beat, without any new position.
suggested_location.access: The temple is beside the Matale to Dambulla road about three kilometres north of Matale town, reached by steps from the roadside; it is a living temple open to visitors, with a small museum and a leaf-book library. Filming inside the caves, in the library and of any leaf writing needs the chief incumbent's permission. The 1974 gazette protection of the inscribed and drip-ledged caves reported elsewhere was not checked for this record. No drone is used. Dress and conduct as for any temple.
suggested_location.best_time: Dry season, a weekday, from mid-morning to closing time. Matale lies in the intermediate zone and gets both monsoons; January to March is the most reliable dry window. The film needs no particular light and avoids sunrise, sunset and poya days, when the temple is busy with worship and should not be filmed for this.

suggested_location.research_note:
District. Matale District stands at 7 on the true count of live films (cross-check of 2026-09-27, which counts IDEA-0062 in Matale), which is closed. This film makes it 8. That is temporary and deliberate: IDEA-0079 (GRP-05, pending) currently also stands at this temple, and that film is to be moved when GRP-05 is reworked, which brings Matale back to 7. IDEA-0079 has been read to keep the two apart and has not been edited. This is also the second GRP-01 film in Matale after IDEA-0003. The reason for spending the district is that this is the only story found anywhere in the island that turns on C018's question; a blind search of the open districts found none.

What was verified and where. The Mahavamsa passage was read in Geiger's 1912 translation (archive.org scan, with verse numbers 100-101 and the notes; no note on the place) and at lakdiva.org.lk. The Dipavamsa passage was read in Oldenberg's 1879 edition and translation (archive.org, XX.20-21, Pali and English). The Pujavaliya sentence was read in the Sinhala text at pitaka.lk (the chapter of royal histories, page 35-2); the Mahinda passage in the preceding chapter (34-7), saying he taught the 84,000 sections of the teaching without bringing a single book from India, 'from the storehouse called his mind', was read and is not used. The Nikaya Sangrahaya was read in the 1908 English translation as republished by ancient-buddhist-texts.net. Buddhaghosa's Culavamsa account was read in Geiger's translation (archive.org OCR, poor but legible). Cave was read in the 1904 edition. Everything about 1848, the 1981-1991 rewriting and 2019 is from modern secondary accounts.

Corrections to what was first read. (1) Popular and newspaper accounts, including the 2019 Sunday Times, say the Pujavaliya records that five hundred monks 'wrote' the Tripitaka at the temple; its verb is saňgāyanā, a recital or council, and it names no district. Writing and the district both first appear, in what was checked, in the Nikaya Sangrahaya. (2) IDEA-0079's historical thread says the Pujavaliya names the venue as 'Aloka-lena or Alu-lena in the Matula district'; the passage checked has Alulena only, with no district and no aloka. (3) IDEA-0079's voice gives famine and invasion as why the monks wrote; neither chronicle gives that reason (it is the people falling away or the decline of beings); the Pujavaliya only places the famine in the same reign. (4) Amazinglanka puts the temple thirty kilometres south of Kandy; it is north. (5) The Buddhaghosa visit 'on record' traces to a 2006 newspaper feature and to Lonely Planet; the Culavamsa does not mention the site. (6) The 1848 burning is not attested in any source from the period that could be reached, and Cave does not mention it in 1897; it is reported here as the later accounts' statement. A blog translation of the Pujavaliya and Nikaya Sangrahaya lines renders pansiyayak as fifty; it means five hundred. None of these corrections was applied to IDEA-0079.

Images. Five files were confirmed on Commons with imageinfo before writing; all are of this temple. The hell-punishment murals (Commons: Hell_Punishments._Aluvihara,_Sri_Lanka_0479.jpg, whose description also says all the images at the site were painted in modern times) are deliberately not used. The 1896 exterior photograph and the other Commons views used by IDEA-0079 were left to that film.

Phase 2 objection, stated against the choice. The strongest objection is that the place is weakest exactly where the film leans on it: the site's role rests on thirteenth- and fourteenth-century texts, a second temple claims the same event, the list the film is about was written down centuries after whatever happened here, and the district is closed and the site already taken. The answer is that the film does not lean on the tradition; it films the tradition as a claim, and the contrast between a place added later and a region with no place at all is the whole argument. The list is never said to have been written here. The district and the shared site are real costs, recorded here and in risks, and are acceptable only because nothing else carries C018; if IDEA-0079 is not moved, this record should go back to Chathura rather than both films standing.

Treatment check. No drone (0001, 0002, 0009 and 0079 use one), no dawn or sunrise payoff (0001, 0079), no tilt into empty air (0002, 0003), no underwater or looking up at a surface (0004), no static wide plus macro and no held uncomfortable frame (0002, 0004, 0006), no continuous descent or single continuous move (0008, 0002), no raking handheld on a wall (0009, 0003), no reverse angle from a facing height (0003), no still drone hover at sunset, solar-noon zenith, heat haze, time-lapse or optical zoom-out. The grammar is a rotation between three fixed stations and two inserts, at ordinary shot lengths, cut roughly in the map's proportions and never pointed out, over one ordinary working day. The ending is a road at closing time, with the voice saying the pictures are not of the fourth region, which differs from the named-but-not-shown line at the end of IDEA-0004 and the spare IDEA-0012.

Not verified. Everything on the ground: permission to film in the caves, the library and the museum; whether any leaf writing is still done here; whether a painted Brahma arch and the four-rivers mural are in the same cave and filmable without lights; whether a bare overhang is accessible; the 1974 gazette notice; the chief incumbent today. No fallback location exists for this slot: the earlier blind search found no other carrier for C018, and the Kegalle temple of the same name is not one (Kegalle stands at 6, it carries only the same tradition, and it was not researched).

unknowns: No permission, participant or access has been confirmed; everything is desk research.
